one_liner: SIMD substring-search kernels (SSE2-AVX512, NEON) from a blog article; beats glibc strstr by ~1.3-1.8x on x86.
what_it_does: Companion source code for 0x80.pl's "SIMD-friendly algorithms for substring searching" article: exact single-needle substring search over a byte buffer, the same problem std::strstr / std::string::find / std::search solve. It is a set of free functions with signature (const char* s, size_t n, const char* needle, size_t k) -> size_t (or std::string overloads), returning the match offset or std::string::npos -- not a packaged library, just loose .cpp/.h kernel files meant to be read or vendored individually. A separate original/ subdirectory holds 32-bit inline-asm code from an earlier 2008 article.
how_it_is_fast: SWAR and SIMD kernels (SSE2, SSE4.1 MPSADBW, SSE4.2 PCMPESTRM, AVX2, AVX512F/BW, NEON) scan 16-64 bytes per iteration instead of glibc strstr's byte-at-a-time loop. The fastest "generic" kernel behind the cited 1.82x number (avx2_strstr_v2 -> avx2_strstr_anysize) broadcasts the needle's first and last byte across a 32-byte AVX2 vector, compares both in one pass to get a lane mask of candidate offsets, then verifies each candidate with a short memcmp -- a vectorized two-byte filter (0x80.pl's "SIMD-friendly Karp-Rabin" scheme), not a per-byte scan. Needles of length 2-12 get separate template-specialized SSE4.1/AVX2 kernels tuned per exact length.
when_to_use: Exact single fixed-needle search over large in-memory byte buffers (logs, text corpora) on x86-64 with SSE4.1/AVX2/AVX512, or ARMv7/AArch64 with NEON, where the scan itself is the bottleneck
You want reference/teaching code for SIMD substring-search techniques (the vectorized Karp-Rabin-style first/last-byte filter) rather than a dependency
You can vendor a handful of individual .cpp/.h files into your own build instead of linking a packaged library
Needle length and target ISA are known ahead of time so you can pick/compile the matching kernel (SSE4, AVX2, AVX512BW, NEON) for your CPU
You're willing to own and patch the code yourself going forward -- no upstream maintenance since Jan 2022
when_not_to_use: You need a drop-in for std::string::find/strstr with wide-char support, custom predicates, or a std::string_view-friendly API -- none of that exists here

You need multi-needle or streaming search; only a single fixed needle against a fully-buffered haystack is implemented (open issue #18 asks for multithreading, #19 for combining with Raita's algorithm -- both unaddressed)
You need a maintained, packaged dependency: no releases, no build-system package config, last commit 2022-01-04, and confirmed bugs (#11, #16) are unfixed
Needle length 1 passed directly to the low-level avx2_strstr_anysize kernel (bypassing the dispatcher) hits a confirmed bug: k-2 underflows (issue #11)
On current hardware/libc the maintainer himself says (issue #12, 2020) "AVX2 won't help much" over a decent modern strstr -- re-benchmark on your own CPU/libc before adopting

integration.dependencies: none (uses <immintrin.h>/<arm_neon.h> intrinsics and the C++11 standard library only)
integration.min_toolchain: C++11; GCC or Clang with the matching ISA flag per kernel (-msse4.2, -mavx2, -mavx512bw, -mfpu=neon)
integration.platforms: x86-64 (SSE2 baseline; SSE4.1/4.2, AVX2, AVX512F/AVX512BW variants gated by build flags), ARMv7 (NEON) and ARMv8/AArch64
integration.thread_safety: not documented -- kernels are pure functions with no shared mutable state, but there is no synchronization code anywhere in the repo, and issue #18 (open) requests multithreading support
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial -- explain: the top-level function signature/return convention mirrors std::string::find (offset or npos) rather than strstr's null-terminated char* return, and using it means vendoring specific kernel files plus manual dispatch by needle length and target ISA rather than including one header

gotchas: Raw per-length kernels (e.g. avx2_strstr_anysize, sse4_strstr_anysize) assert needle_size > 4 or > 0 depending on variant; only the top-level dispatchers (avx2_strstr, avx2_strstr_v2, sse4_strstr_anysize's callers) special-case short needles (0-4 bytes) via strchr/strstr/memcmp -- calling a raw kernel directly with a short needle is unsafe (issue #11, confirmed bug for k=1)

The vectorized loops load fixed 16/32-byte windows (_mm256_loadu_si256 at s+i and s+i+k-1) per iteration, which can read past the logical end of the haystack near its tail; the README/code does not document a guaranteed-safe overread margin, so vendoring into a tightly-sized buffer needs care
Open, unanswered GitHub issue (#16) questions whether the `next1` vector in avx2_strstr_eq (the 2-byte-needle path) is read before being fully initialized

The repo's own speedup.cpp deliberately skips std::string::find on GCC/x86 builds ("proven to be utterly slow, don't waste our time"), so its own benchmark has no std::string::find numbers to compare against on x86
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick this over StringZilla or Boost.Algorithm's Boyer-Moore/Boyer-Moore-Horspool searchers only when you specifically want the raw, ISA-specific kernel source to vendor one function with zero dependencies (no Boost, no StringZilla) or to study the 0x80.pl vectorized Karp-Rabin technique; both siblings are actively packaged and maintained, and StringZilla in particular reports larger, more current speedups over std::string::find.
verified_claims_summary: On an Intel Skylake i7-6700 with GCC 5.4.1 (-O3 -mavx2), the repo's own speedup_avx2 benchmark scanning data/i386.txt for data/words shows glibc std::strstr at 0.662s vs the "AVX2 (generic)" kernel at 0.364s across three runs with identical checksums (~1.82x faster); "SSE2 (generic)" is 0.489s (~1.35x faster). std::string::find is not measured on this run -- the harness skips it on GCC/x86.
status_note: Abandoned: last commit 2022-01-04, not archived, two confirmed/unanswered bugs (#11, #16) unaddressed; BSD-2-Clause and small enough to vendor a single kernel file, but the maintainer himself notes (2020) that on modern CPUs/libc the AVX2 advantage over strstr is small.
